title: Which Classicality? Incidence, Simplex, and Product-Rule Tests in Finite Quantum Logics
abstract: Finite quantum-logical constructions can appear classical or nonclassical depending on which structure is retained. We distinguish incidence tests based on valuations, colorings, and partition representations; simplex-embedding tests for specified prepare-and-measure fragments; and operator-functional tests imposing spectral and product rules. We show that the collective GHZ joint measurement is a single Boolean context and becomes nonclassical only when a common assignment of local factors, together with product preservation, is required. For selected labelled ray fragments, we compute state-depolarizing thresholds for a restricted projector-cone factorization and for a specified vector-generated operational closure, separating exact primal--dual certificates from numerical estimates. These values are properties of the stated fragments and noise model, not invariants of the underlying hypergraphs or a universal ordering of contextuality.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theory distinguishing between different forms of 'classicality' failure in quantum logics by employing three distinct mathematical tests: incidence, simplex-embedding, and operator-functional rules. The central finding is that the observed nonclassicality depends entirely on which structural assumptions (e.g., requiring product preservation) are imposed during the analysis. It provides a powerful framework for understanding contextuality beyond simple Bell inequalities.
main_problem: The core problem is determining when quantum logical structures (contexts) exhibit genuine nonclassicality, as this property depends critically on which mathematical structure—incidence, convex-operational, or operator-algebraic—is retained.
main_result: Classicality is shown to be a 'bookkeeping choice' dependent on the structural data used for testing; specific quantum violations (like GHZ) only emerge when global product rules are imposed beyond local context measurements.
method: The authors distinguish and apply three types of tests: incidence tests (based on valuations/colorings), simplex-embedding tests (for prepare-and-measure fragments), and operator-functional tests (imposing spectral/product rules).
model_or_system: The study uses abstract finite quantum logics, modeling contexts via Boolean blocks $\{P_1, \dots, P_d\}$ which can be viewed as partitions or Projection-Valued Measures (PVMs) in a physical realization.
key_observables: Detector-click frequencies ($p_i$), contextuality strength, and the existence of exact primal/dual certificates for various logical configurations ($\Gamma_3$, Specker bug).
important_parameters: The results are highly dependent on the specific labeled ray fragments, noise models (e.g., state-side depolarizing noise), and the chosen factorization structure.
main_assumptions: The analysis carefully distinguishes between 'bare two-context statistics' (which can be classical) and scenarios requiring global constraints or product preservation rules.
figures_summary: References computational tables comparing various logical configurations, detailing whether exact primal or dual certificates exist for simplex embeddability tests.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the diagnostic power of three distinct mathematical frameworks—incidence (combinatorial), simplex-embedding (operational/convex geometry), and product-rule preservation (algebraic)—to characterize contextuality failure modes.
why_interesting: While not directly focused on AMO Hamiltonians, the rigorous framework for testing contextuality by separating structural assumptions (e.g., local factor vs. global measurement) provides deep theoretical tools applicable to understanding nonclassical correlations in quantum measurements relevant to open systems or entanglement verification.
